steps.detail: Carbonate hardness = the smaller of (total hardness, alkalinity). Non-carbonate hardness = total hardness - carbonate hardness. The key relationship here is $\text{Hardness as CaCO}_3=C\times\text{conversion factor}$.

steps.title: Find carbonate hardness
steps.detail: min(310, 180) = 180 mg/L. The key relationship here is $\text{Hardness as CaCO}_3=C\times\text{conversion factor}$.

steps.title: Find non-carbonate hardness
steps.detail: 310 - 180. The key relationship here is $\text{Hardness as CaCO}_3=C\times\text{conversion factor}$.

steps.title: Answer
steps.detail: The completed calculation gives $\boxed{\text{130 mg/L}}$ as the correct result.

shortcut: Convert each ion to mg/L as CaCO$_3$ first, then add contributions or compare hardness with alkalinity as appropriate.

hint: This is a units-conversion problem using the ideal gas law in disguise - concentration by mass needs to become concentration by volume (moles).
question: A benzene vapor sample has a concentration of 1,850 mg/m3 at room temperature (25°C, 1 atm). Benzene's molecular weight is 78 g/mol. What is this concentration in ppmV (parts per million by volume)? (Use the molar volume of an ideal gas at 25°C, 1 atm: 24.45 L/mol)
explanation: Convert mg/m3 to mol/m3: 1850 mg/m3 / 78,000 mg/mol = 0.0237 mol/m3. Convert to volume fraction: 0.0237 mol/m3 x 24.45 L/mol = 0.579 L of benzene vapor per m3 (1000 L) of air = 579 ppmV.

steps.title: Convert mass concentration to molar concentration
steps.detail: 0.0237 mol/m3 = 1,850 mg/m3 ÷ 78,000 mg/mol (78 g/mol converted to mg/mol). The key relationship here is $ppm_V=(\text{mol gas}/\text{mol air})\times10^6$.

steps.title: Convert moles to an equivalent gas volume using molar volume
steps.detail: 0.0237 mol/m3 x 24.45 L/mol = 0.579 L of benzene vapor per m3 of air. The key relationship here is $ppm_V=(\text{mol gas}/\text{mol air})\times10^6$.

steps.title: Convert that volume ratio to ppmV
steps.detail: 0.579 L per 1,000 L of air = 579 parts per million by volume. The key relationship here is $ppm_V=(\text{mol gas}/\text{mol air})\times10^6$.

steps.title: Answer
steps.detail: The completed calculation gives $\boxed{\text{580 ppmV}}$ as the correct result.

concept: A gas concentration reported by mass per volume can be converted to a volume fraction by using molecular weight and the gas molar volume.
shortcut: At 25°C and 1 atm, use the 24.45 L/mol molar volume to turn mol/m$^3$ into a gas volume fraction.
gotcha: The trap is confusing mg/m$^3$ with ppmV; ppmV requires a molar-to-volume conversion.

hint: For a freely discharging opening, the water depth above the opening provides the driving head, and the real opening is represented by a discharge coefficient.
question: A 2-inch diameter orifice in the side of a tank discharges freely to atmosphere. The water surface is 9 ft above the orifice centerline. A discharge coefficient of 0.61 and g = 32.2 ft/s2 apply. What is the discharge rate?

steps.title: Find the orifice area
steps.detail: $D = 2\ \text{in} = 0.1667\ \text{ft}$, so $A = \dfrac{\pi D^2}{4} \approx 0.0218\ \text{ft}^2$

steps.title: Find the ideal (theoretical) velocity from the driving head
steps.detail: This is the same $v=\sqrt{2gh}$ relationship as a ball falling height $h$: $v = \sqrt{2 \times 32.2 \times 9} \approx 24.07\ \text{ft/s}$

steps.title: Apply the discharge coefficient to get the actual flow
steps.detail: Real orifices contract the jet and add friction, so multiply by $C_d = 0.61$: $Q = C_d \times A \times v = 0.61 \times 0.0218 \times 24.07$

steps.title: Compute
steps.detail: The completed calculation gives $\boxed{\text{0.32 cfs}}$ as the correct result.

concept: Water leaves the tank because gravity converts the elevation head above the opening into exit speed, with the real opening losing some of the ideal flow to contraction and friction.

water surface

             ↓ discharges freely to atmosphere
shortcut: For a sharp-edged opening, $Q=C_dA\sqrt{2gh}$; convert diameter to feet before finding area.
gotcha: The trap is using the tank depth as a pressure directly without converting it to the velocity-driving head and accounting for $C_d$.

question: A treatment basin has a 1.2 MG volume and a flow of 3.6 MGD. If the desired detention time is 8 hours, is the basin adequately sized?
explanation: Yes; the actual detention time is 8 hours.
concept: Convert 0.333 day to hours before comparing with the target.

steps.title: Compare with the target
steps.detail: The actual and desired detention times are equal, so the basin meets the stated target.

shortcut: Do not compare days directly to an hourly target.

question: A sample set gives repeated readings of 98, 99, 98, and 99 when the accepted reference value is 110. How should the measurements be described?
explanation: The measurements are inaccurate but precise.
concept: Accuracy compares to truth; precision compares readings to each other.

steps.title: Assess accuracy
steps.detail: The readings cluster around 98–99 but the reference is 110, so they are far from the true/accepted value.

steps.title: Assess precision
steps.detail: The readings are tightly clustered, so they are repeatable. $\boxed{\text{inaccurate but precise}}$

shortcut: Do not call a tightly clustered set accurate merely because it is consistent.

question: A contaminant has an initial dissolved concentration of 80 mg/L and follows first-order decay with a half-life of 4 years. What is the concentration after 8 years?
concept: Count half-lives before calculating.

steps.title: Recognize the time pattern
steps.detail: Eight years equals two half-lives of four years each.

steps.title: Apply the repeated reduction
steps.detail: After one half-life: 40 mg/L. After two: 20 mg/L. Wait: starting at 80, two half-lives gives $80(1/2)^2=20\,mg/L$. $\boxed{C=20\,mg/L}$

shortcut: Do not halve only once when two half-lives have elapsed.
